P1e: In every community there was somebody who took the initiative to get it started. Somebody had to find the land, write the first documents, teach the method, recruit the first members, or even just keep things going when others lost interest.
P2e: This person will always have real influence on the group. Denying it just makes that influence harder to look at.
P5e: Allow for parallel implementations. Fork the method. If the community finds a way to alter Hearthwork and get better results, they've taught me something. If it needs the founder's “blessing”, then it's not really running in parallel, is it?
P7e: Can the community override the founder, with all due respect? Can the community replace the role of the founder? Can the community alter the vision of the founder? Can the community exist without the founder?
P8d: Then follow the practical power. Whose name is on the deed? Who's in charge of the housing and the food stores, the vehicles and tools, and any bank account outside the community? Who keeps the records? Who decides who gets admitted, and who picks the reviewers? Who controls access to the kids and to medicine, and who can make a complaint go away? The org chart might look flat and horizontal, while the keys, passwords, titles and even just general reputation all point to one person.
P11e: Also watch for the daily signs. Increasing focus on the founder over time. Sense that disagreement is failure. Bad results are blamed on lack of good implementation. Increasing “insider” knowledge. Decreasing public accountability. Failure to measure results. Sense that those who leave are morally contaminated.
P12e: Presence of one or more of these isn't proof of abuse, but if several are present, they are worth paying attention to before the founder can explain how the situation is uniquely different in a spiritual way.
P15e: Peer counseling can be turned into peer surveillance, even with a warm tone. Requiring practices like that as prerequisites for medicine can create gatekeepers who have power over people when they are most open. Even the idea of “willing to be seen” can be used to demand that people disclose to the group whatever the group wants them to.
P16e: The boundary is simple. These aren't things that give the community power over me, they are simply a set of principles I am attempting to live up to.
P17e: “Nothing suppressed” applies to myself and my relationship with my own material. It doesn't give anyone the right to pull anything out of me. Any member can choose not to share material, and they don't need to provide a therapeutic rationale for not sharing.
P18e: The medicine is optional. Choosing not to take the medicine in no way affects anyone's rights as a member. The right to let people into the group is not vested in any individual or permanent clique. And disagreement gets answered as disagreement.
P19e: “Your resistance is just your wound talking” is pretty much a conversation ender. Once you notice a community diagnosing dissent like this instead of answering it, leave. Better yet, leave before it even gets to the point of people wanting to do group process about your leaving.
P20e: You should not be expected to give up your bodily safety, access to enough food and sleep, independent medical care, the ability to think privately, contact with people outside the community, a way to report harm without asking the accused person's friends for permission, or the ability to leave, even if the majority of the community votes that you should. It's not consent, no matter how many people in the community vote to tell you that it is.
